message.content:
The sea doesn’t have a single, fixed color—it changes with light, depth, water composition, and the environment around it.

| Factor | Typical Effect on Color |
|--------|------------------------|
| **Depth** | Shallow water reflects more of the sky, often looking turquoise or pale blue. Deeper water absorbs longer wavelengths (red, orange) and scatters shorter ones (blue, green), giving a deep blue or even indigo hue. |
| **Clarity** | Clear water lets sunlight penetrate deeper, so you see a richer blue. Turbid or muddy water scatters light differently, often giving a greenish or brownish tint. |
| **Algae & Phytoplankton** | High concentrations of green algae can make the water look green or even a vivid emerald. |
| **Sun Angle & Weather** | A bright, clear day can make the sea look bright blue; overcast skies or sunrise/sunset can give it a golden or pinkish glow. |
| **Substrate** | A sandy bottom reflects light back up, brightening the surface; a rocky or vegetated bottom can darken it. |

So, while we often think of the sea as “blue,” its actual color is a dynamic blend of physics, biology, and environment—ranging from turquoise and green to deep indigo and even brownish tones depending on where and when you look.
